opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most interesting open questions right now. If you look at what made AlphaGo and AlphaZero so strong, it wasn't just the policy network. It was pairing a good learned intuition with explicit lookahead: Monte Carlo tree search, rolling forward, checking whether your gut feeling holds up a few moves deep. A lot of people have wondered why language models don't do something analogous.

What's happened with the reasoning models is interesting. In a sense they've learned to do search *implicitly*, inside the chain of thought. When a model writes "wait, let me reconsider," or tries an approach, notices it fails, and backtracks, that's a linearized tree search. The model is simulating branches in text rather than us bolting an external search procedure on top. And empirically that's worked better than a lot of the explicit approaches people tried, like tree-of-thoughts or MCTS over tokens. Part of the reason is that language is a very flexible medium for search. You don't need a fixed branching factor or a hand-designed state representation. The model decides what's worth exploring and at what level of abstraction.

The bottleneck, in my view, is the simulator, or really the value function. In Go you have a perfect simulator: the rules of the game. You always know exactly what state results from a move, and at the end you get an unambiguous win or loss. In math and code you get some of that, because you can run the code or check the proof, which is why reasoning has taken off fastest there. But for open-ended reasoning about the real world, like "what happens if this company does X" or "how will this molecule behave," the model has to be its own simulator, and its world model may be wrong in ways it can't detect. Searching harder over a flawed simulator can make things worse. You end up exploiting the model's errors, finding plans that look great in imagination and fall apart in reality.

So I think the prospects depend a lot on grounding. The exciting direction is coupling forward simulation in the model's head with cheap real-world checks: running experiments, executing code, querying tools, and in robotics, actually trying things physically or in a high-fidelity learned simulator. World models for robotics are interesting here because you can do video-prediction-style rollouts, imagine what happens if the arm does this, and then verify against reality and keep correcting the model.

Long term, I suspect the distinction between "the model reasoning" and "the model searching" disappears. It'll just be a system that allocates more thinking to harder problems, imagines consequences, and gets better at knowing when its own imagination can be trusted. That last part, calibrated self-knowledge about when your simulation is reliable, is the piece I'd watch most closely.

r001.rationale: It describes models exploring and backtracking within chain of thought as an implicit, linearized search, without an external search procedure.

r002.rationale: It presents lookahead as a way to check intuitions and identifies the simulator or value function as central to evaluating reasoning, with real-world checks to ground predictions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's two camps here, and I've gone back and forth between them. One camp says: the model should explicitly roll out futures, build a tree, score the leaves, back up the values — basically bring AlphaZero-style search to language. And on paper that's really attractive, because search is this beautiful way to convert compute into capability without needing more data.

The problem is that in Go you have a perfect simulator and a crisp reward. In most of the stuff we actually care about — writing code, doing research, running a robot — you don't. The "simulator" is the model's own world model, and the world model is wrong in exactly the places where search would matter most. So you end up with a search that's very confident about exploring a tree that doesn't correspond to reality. I've seen this with robotics: you plan in your learned dynamics model, you find some gorgeous trajectory, and it's gorgeous precisely because it exploits the errors in the model.

The other camp — and this is where I've landed more recently — is that chain of thought is already search, it's just amortized. When a model writes "wait, let me reconsider," that's backtracking. When it enumerates three approaches and picks one, that's branching. It's a linear text serialization of a tree, and the nice thing is the model learned what to expand from the data and from RL, rather than from a hand-designed heuristic like UCB. My suspicion is that explicit tree search mostly gets eaten by this. Every time people have bolted structure on top of a sequence model, the bitter lesson shows up and the sequence model just learns the structure itself if you give it enough compute.

Where I think forward simulation genuinely survives is when you can get a real signal from the environment cheaply. Code is the obvious one — you can actually run it. Math with a verifier. Agents where you can sandbox an action and see what happens. In those domains, "simulation" isn't the model imagining the future, it's the model actually executing in the future and reading the result back in, and that's enormously powerful because it grounds you. So I'd rephrase the question: the future isn't "search inside the LLM," it's the LLM as a policy that knows when to go touch the world versus when to just think harder in text. And learning that tradeoff — how many tokens to spend, when to roll out, when to commit — I think that's the real frontier, and it's going to be learned, not engineered.

r001.rationale: It describes chain of thought as amortized search, with reconsideration as backtracking and enumerated approaches as branching, while noting the model can learn this structure without explicit tree search.

r002.rationale: It presents forward rollouts with scored leaves and backed-up values as a way to use search, and says real environmental feedback can ground simulation and make it powerful, despite noting limitations.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential there. One way to think about it is that a language model gives you a very powerful proposal distribution: given a problem, what are some promising things to try? But proposing a good action and knowing whether that action will work are different capabilities. Search lets you spend additional computation on that second part.

The important question is: what are you searching against? In programming, you can write some code, execute it, and get feedback. You have something outside the model that tells you whether your prediction was correct. That makes search much more useful. If you’re reasoning about a business decision, and the model is both proposing the strategy and simulating how everyone will respond, it can construct a very convincing trajectory that’s completely wrong.

So I’d distinguish searching over possible answers from simulating the consequences of actions. You can do the former even with a fairly weak world model, provided you have a good verifier. The latter really depends on the fidelity of your simulator. Searching harder in an inaccurate simulator can just find increasingly clever ways to exploit its inaccuracies.

What’s exciting is the possibility of learning from that process. You spend a lot of compute exploring, find a solution that you wouldn’t have produced in one shot, and then train the model to produce that solution more directly. Search improves the policy, and a better policy makes the next round of search more efficient. I think that feedback loop is very promising. The harder question is how broadly we can get reliable feedback outside domains where answers are easy to check.

r001.rationale: The response discusses search and simulation but does not say LLMs can reason in a human-like way without an explicit tree structure.

r002.rationale: It explains that search can spend extra computation checking whether proposed actions work, while simulation can assess their consequences; both can help evaluate candidate actions during reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of promise there, but the key question is: what tells you that one branch of the search is better than another? Generating more candidate answers is relatively straightforward. Reliably evaluating them is the hard part.

In something like chess, you have a simulator that gives you exact transitions, and the rules tell you when you’ve won. For a language model reasoning about the world, the simulator is often the model itself. So if it has a misconception, doing more search can just elaborate on that misconception. You get a very detailed argument built on a false premise.

That makes me particularly excited about domains where you can close the loop with something external. With code, you can execute it. With math, sometimes you can check a proof. The model proposes something, gets feedback, and revises it. Search has something solid to push against.

But I don’t think the end state is necessarily to do this enormous search for every question. You’d want to take the successful trajectories and train the model on them, so that something that required a lot of deliberation initially becomes an intuition. Then you spend your search budget on the next thing you don’t already know how to do. That interplay between learning and search seems more powerful to me than either one in isolation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses search and evaluation but does not mention apparently human-like reasoning or the absence of an explicit tree structure.

r002.rationale: It says the key question is how to tell which search branch is better and describes external feedback from executing code or checking proofs as a way to evaluate candidates during reasoning.
